question: The Work-Energy theorem states that the total work done on an object is equal to:

options.text: Change in the work and energy of the body
Change in the potential energy of the body
Change in the kinetic energy of the body
Change in the static energy of the body

solution:
The correct answer is __**Change in the kinetic energy of the body**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Work-Energy Theorem** states that the **net work done** by the sum of all forces acting on an object is equal to the **change in the kinetic energy** of that object.
 
• This principle is derived from **Newton's Second Law of Motion** and is applicable to both **constant** and **variable forces**. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• Mathematically, the theorem can be expressed as **W = ΔK**, where **W** is the **total work done** and **ΔK** is the **change in kinetic energy** (Final KE - Initial KE).
 
• The formula for **Kinetic Energy (KE)** is **1/2 mv²**, where **m** represents the **mass** of the body and **v** represents its **velocity**.
 
• If the **net work** done on an object is **positive**, its **kinetic energy increases**, meaning the object speeds up. If the **net work** is **negative**, the **kinetic energy decreases**, and the object slows down.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Work Done:**
 
 
• In **physics**, **work** is done when a **force** acts upon an object to cause a **displacement**. It is a **scalar quantity**.
 
• The **SI unit** of work is the **Joule (J)**, which is equivalent to **1 Newton-meter (N·m)**.
 
• The formula for work is **W = Fd cosθ**, where **F** is force, **d** is displacement, and **θ** is the angle between the force and displacement vectors.
 
 
 
• **Potential Energy (PE):**
 
 
• **Potential Energy** is the energy held by an object because of its **position** relative to other objects, stresses within itself, or its **electric charge**.
 
• The most common form is **Gravitational Potential Energy**, calculated as **PE = mgh**, where **g** is the **acceleration due to gravity** (approximately **9.8 m/s²** on Earth) and **h** is the **height**.
 
 
 
• **Kinetic Energy (KE):**
 
 
• It is the energy that a body possesses by virtue of being in **motion**. 
 
• Since it depends on the **square of the velocity**, kinetic energy is always a **non-negative** value.
 
 
 
• **Law of Conservation of Energy:**
 
 
• This law states that **energy** can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be **transformed** from one form to another.
 
• In a **closed system** where only **conservative forces** act, the sum of **Kinetic Energy** and **Potential Energy** remains **constant**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Scalar Nature:** Both **Work** and **Energy** are **scalar quantities**, meaning they have magnitude but no **direction**.
 
• **Power:** The **rate** at which **work** is done or **energy** is transferred is called **Power**. Its **SI unit** is the **Watt (W)**, where **1 Watt = 1 Joule per second**.
 
• **Static Energy:** This usually refers to **Electrostatic Energy** (energy stored in an electric field) or potential energy in a stationary state, but it is not the primary component defined by the **Work-Energy Theorem**.
 
• **Applications:** The **Work-Energy Theorem** is widely used in **engineering** and **mechanics** to solve problems where **force** and **displacement** are known, avoiding the need to calculate **acceleration** via **Newton's Second Law**.
